mcqs.question: Why does greedy decoding tend to produce repetitive, bland text?
options: It always picks the locally most-likely token, which can trap it into re-selecting an already-likely phrase instead of exploring other viable continuations
It has a bug that duplicates tokens after generation finishes
It only works correctly on very short prompts
It applies a repetition penalty that is too weak by default
mcqs.explanation: Greedy decoding commits to the single top token at every step with no randomness, so once a phrase becomes locally probable it keeps getting picked again, producing loops. It's not a bug, a prompt-length limit, or a penalty setting — it's an inherent property of always taking the argmax.

mcqs.question: Setting temperature to a high value (e.g. 1.5) does what to the next-token distribution?
options: Sharpens it toward the single most likely token, making output more deterministic
Flattens it, giving lower-probability tokens a relatively higher chance of being sampled
Has no effect on sampling, only on the model's training loss
Converts sampling into beam search automatically
mcqs.explanation: Dividing logits by a temperature greater than 1 flattens the softmax distribution, boosting the relative chance of less-likely tokens and increasing output variety. A temperature below 1 does the opposite (sharpens); temperature affects sampling at inference, not training loss, and has nothing to do with beam search.

mcqs.question: Why is top-p (nucleus) sampling generally preferred over a fixed top-k?
options: Top-p is computationally cheaper because it never sorts the vocabulary
Top-p guarantees the output is factually correct
Top-p's candidate pool size adapts to how confident or uncertain the model is at each step, while top-k always keeps a fixed count regardless of the distribution's shape
Top-k cannot be combined with temperature, while top-p can
mcqs.explanation: Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability crosses a threshold, so the pool naturally narrows when the model is confident and widens when it's uncertain — top-k's fixed count can't adapt that way. Both require some sorting/cumulative work, neither guarantees factual correctness, and both compose fine with temperature.

mcqs.question: Why is beam search rarely used for open-ended chat generation despite finding a higher joint-probability sequence than greedy decoding?
options: Beam search is always slower than sampling by several orders of magnitude, making it infeasible
Beam search only works for classification tasks, not generation
Beam search cannot be implemented for autoregressive models
The highest joint-probability sequence in open-ended generation tends to be the safest, blandest, most repetitive option, which reads worse than a sampled one
mcqs.explanation: For open-ended tasks with many acceptable outputs, the globally highest-probability sequence found by beam search is often generic and repetitive — variety, not the single best-scoring path, is what makes chat or creative text feel good, which is why sampling methods took over there. Beam search is more expensive but not infeasible, and it works fine with autoregressive decoders — it's just a poor fit for open-ended tasks.

mcqs.question: Given next-token probabilities {"the": 0.5, "a": 0.3, "an": 0.15, "this": 0.05}, what happens under top-p (nucleus) sampling with p=0.9?
options: All four tokens remain in the sampling pool with their original probabilities
Only "the" remains, since it alone exceeds 50% probability
"the", "a", and "an" remain (cumulative 0.95), "this" is dropped, and the remaining three are renormalized
The pool is fixed at exactly 2 tokens regardless of the probabilities
mcqs.explanation: Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. Summing in order (0.5, 0.3, 0.15) crosses 0.9 at 0.95 with three tokens, so "this" (which would push it to 1.0) is excluded and the remaining three are renormalized. It doesn't keep all four, isn't limited to just the single top token, and doesn't fix the pool size the way top-k does.

mcqs.question: Why can an API call with temperature=0 still occasionally return different output for the identical prompt?
options: Batched GPU inference can have non-deterministic floating-point summation order, which can flip a near-tied top token and cascade into a different generation
Temperature=0 is silently ignored by most providers
Temperature=0 actually increases randomness instead of removing it
The vocabulary itself changes between requests
mcqs.explanation: Temperature=0 removes sampling randomness, but production serving batches requests, and floating-point operations aren't guaranteed bit-identical across different batch compositions — a rare near-tie can flip, and that single flip propagates through the rest of the generation. Providers don't ignore the setting, it doesn't increase randomness, and the vocabulary is fixed.
